ABSTRACT 
Industrial workplaces routinely expose personnel to potentially hazardous 
concentrations of toxic gases including nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), carbon monoxide (CO), and 
sulfur dioxide (SO₂), while simultaneously experiencing unpredictable fluctuations in 
temperature, relative humidity, and overall air quality. Traditional monitoring approaches 
depend on bulky, single-parameter instruments that are neither portable nor capable of 
delivering immediate on-site alerts, leaving workers vulnerable during the critical interval 
between hazard onset and control-room response. 
This project presen

delivering immediate on-site alerts, leaving workers vulnerable during the critical interval 
between hazard onset and control-room response. 
This project presents the design and hardware implementation of a Compact Embedded 
Monitoring System (CEMS) for industrial hazard detection. The system is built around the 
ESP32 microcontroller, which continuously acquires readings from MQ-series metal-oxide 
semiconductor gas sensors and a DHT22 temperature-humidity transducer. Sensor data are 
processed locally, visualised on a dual OLED display, broadcast to a lightweight web 
dashboard over Wi-Fi, and — when user-defined safety thresholds are breached — 
communicated through an audible buzzer and indicator LEDs. 
The proposed system overcomes the key limitations of existing solutions by integrating 
multi-parameter sensing, local real-time visualisation, wireless remote monitoring, and 
threshold-based alerting within a single low-cost, portable housin

ations of existing solutions by integrating 
multi-parameter sensing, local real-time visualisation, wireless remote monitoring, and 
threshold-based alerting within a single low-cost, portable housing. Bench-level testing 
demonstrates stable multi-parameter acquisition, sub-second alert latency, and sustained 
operation across simulated industrial load cycles, confirming suitability for further field trials 
in manufacturing and chemical-processing environments. 
The project contributes a replicable, open-hardware reference design that can be readily 
extended with additional sensing modalities, cloud connectivity, and enhanced data logging 
for comprehensive industrial safety management. 
 
 
Keywords: Embedded systems, industrial safety, gas detection, ESP32, MQ-series sensors, 
OLED display, real-time monitoring, IoT, hazard alert.

CHAPTER 1 
INTRODUCTION 
1.1  Background and Motivation 
Industrial workplaces — including manufacturing plants, petrochemical refineries, 
power generation facilities, and mining operations — are environments where personnel are 
routinely exposed to a complex mixture of airborne chemical and physical hazards. Among the 
most prevalent and dangerous of these hazards are toxic gases, particularly carbon monoxide 
(CO), nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), and sulfur dioxide (SO₂). Each of these substances poses a 
distinct and serious threat to human health.

of these hazards are toxic gases, particularly carbon monoxide 
(CO), nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), and sulfur dioxide (SO₂). Each of these substances poses a 
distinct and serious threat to human health. Carbon monoxide binds preferentially to 
haemoglobin and disrupts cellular oxygen transport, causing symptoms ranging from headache 
and dizziness at low concentrations to unconsciousness and death at high exposures. Nitrogen 
dioxide is a powerful oxidant that attacks the respiratory epithelium, causing pulmonary 
oedema and long-term lung damage. Sulfur dioxide dissolves in the mucous membranes of the 
upper respiratory tract, producing sulfurous acid and triggering severe bronchospasm. 
Beyond gas-phase hazards, ambient thermal and humidity conditions profoundly affect 
both worker physiology and process safety. Elevated temperature and humidity increase the 
physiological strain on workers, impairing cognitive performance and physical endurance. 
Extreme temperatures also accelerate de

gy and process safety. Elevated temperature and humidity increase the 
physiological strain on workers, impairing cognitive performance and physical endurance. 
Extreme temperatures also accelerate degradation of electrical insulation, increase the 
volatility of flammable solvents, and alter the kinetics of chemical reactions within process 
equipment in ways that can amplify risk. The simultaneous monitoring of multiple 
environmental parameters is therefore not merely a regulatory formality but a genuine 
operational necessity for safe and reliable industrial activity. 
1.2  Problem Statement 
Current industrial monitoring infrastructure addresses these hazards only partially and 
often inadequately. Dedicated fixed-point gas analysers, while analytically precise, are 
expensive capital items that require permanent installation, specialist calibration, and 
transmission of data to centralised control rooms. This architecture introduces a 
communication latency that can be critical i

transmission of data to centralised control rooms. This architecture introduces a 
communication latency that can be critical in fast-developing accident scenarios, and fixed 
locations cannot track personnel who move through different zones of a plant.

Portable single-gas personal detectors carried by individual workers are limited to a 
single analyte and provide no consolidated situational picture for supervisors or safety officers. 
Research prototypes reported in the published literature have explored microcontroller-based 
multi-sensor platforms with varying degrees of success, yet these systems commonly retain 
dependencies on cloud connectivity, external server infrastructure, or single-display hardware, 
rendering them unsuitable for the network-constrained, electrically noisy conditions 
encountered in heavy industry.

There is therefore a clearly identified gap for a compact, self-contained embedded 
device that can simultaneously monitor multiple gas species and ambient environmental 
parameters, present data locally in real time without depending on external infrastructure, and 
issue immediate alerts when safety boundaries are crossed. 
1.3  Objectives 
The primary objectives of this project are: 
1. To design a compact embedded monitoring device centred on the ESP32 
microcontroller that acquires real-time data from gas and environmental sensors 
simultaneously. 
2. To integrate MQ-series metal-oxide semiconductor sensors for CO, NO₂, and SO₂ 
detection alongside a DHT22 transducer for temperature and relative humidity 
measurement. 
3. To provide immediate local visualisation of all parameters on dual OLED displ

detection alongside a DHT22 transducer for temperature and relative humidity 
measurement. 
3. To provide immediate local visualisation of all parameters on dual OLED displays, 
ensuring that personnel can read safety-critical information without requiring network 
connectivity. 
4. To implement threshold-based alerting via audible buzzer and LED indicators, with 
sub-second latency from hazard onset to alert assertion. 
5. To broadcast sensor data to a lightweight web dashboard served directly from the 
ESP32 over Wi-Fi, enabling wireless remote monitoring without reliance on cloud 
platforms. 
6. To validate the prototype through systematic bench-level testing covering sensor 
accuracy, alert latency, power consumption, and operational stability.

1.4  Scope of the Project 
This project encompasses the complete hardware design, firmware development, and 
bench-level experimental validation of the CEMS prototype. The scope includes component 
selection and characterisation, circuit integration, ESP32 firmware implementation using the 
Arduino framework, OLED display driver integration, web server implementation, and 
threshold-alert logic. The scope explicitly excludes regulatory certification, long-term field 
deployment beyond laboratory soak testing, and integration with plant-level SCADA or 
distributed control systems, which are identified as directions for future work.

2.1  Early Gas Detection Systems 
The systematic detection of hazardous industrial gases has a history extending back to 
the early twentieth century, when the Davy safety lamp was adapted to detect methane in coal 
mines by observing changes in flame height. Th

concentrations by measuring the current produced during controlled redox reactions at inert

Metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) sensors, commercialised following pioneering

characterised by low cost, mechanical robustness, and broad-spectrum response to reducing

MQTT-based communication protocols have been explored as an alternative to HTTP 
REST APIs for transmitting sensor data, offering lower overhead and publish-subscribe 
semantics suited to multi-device deployments. However, MQTT still requires a reachable 
broker, typically hosted in the cloud or on a local server, which again introduces infrastructure 
dependencies. The approach adopted in the proposed CEMS system — hosting an HTTP server 
directly on the ESP32 — eliminates all external dependencies at the cost of limiting concurrent 
client connections, a trade-off considered acceptable for the targeted single-zone monitoring 
application.

2.4  Multi-Parameter Integrated Systems 
Raj et al. combined a DHT11 temperature-humidity sensor with an MQ-135 gas sensor 
on an ESP8266, providing the first demonstration — in the accessible academic literature —

for the current work.

CHAPTER 3 
SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY 
3.1  System Overview 
The Compact Embedded Monitoring System (CEMS) is structured as a layered sensing 
and output architecture centred on the ESP32 microcontroller. The sensing layer comprises 
three parallel channels: an MQ-7 module targeting CO, an MQ-135 module providi

ructured as a layered sensing 
and output architecture centred on the ESP32 microcontroller. The sensing layer comprises 
three parallel channels: an MQ-7 module targeting CO, an MQ-135 module providing 
broadband response to NO₂ and SO₂ analogues, and a DHT22 transducer measuring 
temperature and relative humidity. The processing layer, implemented as firmware on the 
ESP32, applies calibration transforms to raw sensor readings and evaluates each value against 
configurable safety thresholds. The output layer consists of three parallel output paths: local 
display on dual OLED screens, wireless transmission to a locally hosted web dashboard, and 
physical alerting via buzzer and LED. 
This architecture was chosen to ensure that all primary safety functions — sensing, 
processing, local display, and alerting — operate independently of network connectivity. The 
wireless dashboard represents a supplementary monitoring capability that enhances situational 
awareness for supervisors but i

splay, and alerting — operate independently of network connectivity. The 
wireless dashboard represents a supplementary monitoring capability that enhances situational 
awareness for supervisors but is not required for the core safety function. This design 
philosophy distinguishes the CEMS from cloud-dependent systems reviewed in the literature 
survey. 
3.2  Hardware Components 
3.2.1  ESP32-WROOM-32 Microcontroller 
The ESP32-WROOM-32 module from Espressif Systems was selected as the host 
controller on account of its dual-core Xtensa LX6 processor operating at up to 240 MHz, 520 
KB integrated SRAM, 4 MB SPI flash, eighteen-channel twelve-bit SAR ADC, integrated 
802.11 b/g/n Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 4.2 transceivers, and hardware I²C and SPI controllers. The 
dual-core architecture is particularly advantageous: one core handles time-critical sensor 
acquisition and display refresh tasks, while the second manages the Wi-Fi stack and HTTP 
server without introducing latency into the sens

icularly advantageous: one core handles time-critical sensor 
acquisition and display refresh tasks, while the second manages the Wi-Fi stack and HTTP 
server without introducing latency into the sensing loop.

3.2.2  MQ-7 Carbon Monoxide Sensor 
The MQ-7 is a metal-oxide semiconductor sensor employing a heated SnO₂ sensing 
element whose surface conductivity decreases upon adsorption of CO molecules. The sensor 
module includes an on-board comparator with adjustable potentiometer, providing both an 
analogue voltage proportional to gas concentration and a digital threshold output. The

module includes an on-board comparator with adjustable potentiometer, providing both an 
analogue voltage proportional to gas concentration and a digital threshold output. The 
measurement range specified by the manufacturer is 20–2000 ppm CO, with a sensitivity 
defined as the resistance ratio Rs/R0 changing from approximately 0.9 to 0.1 over this 
concentration range. Sensor warm-up requires a 48-hour burn-in period for stable baseline 
establishment. 
3.2.3  MQ-135 Broadband Gas Sensor 
The MQ-135 sensor shares the same SnO₂ MOS architecture as the MQ-7 but is

nitrogen-containing compounds. While it does not provide single-analyte selectivity for NO₂

.2.4  DHT22 Temperature and Humidity Sensor 
The DHT22 (AM2302) capacitive sensor measures temperature across –40 to +80°C 
with a specified accuracy of ±0.5°C, and relative humidity from 0 to 100% RH with ±2–5% 
RH accuracy. Its factory-calibrated single-wire digital protocol delivers sixteen-bit resolution 
data at a maximum update rate of 0.5 Hz. A 4.7 kΩ pull-up resistor on the data line ensures 
signal integrity over the 15 cm connection to the ESP32.

3.2.5  Dual SSD1306 OLED Displays 
Two monochrome 0.96-inch SSD1306 OLED modules connected in parallel on the I²C 
bus at addresses 0x3C and 0x3D constitute the local user interface. The SSD1306 controller 
communicates at up to 400 kHz in fast-mode I²C, permitting a display refresh rate of 
approximately 10 Hz for the 128×64 pixel array. Screen 1 presents temperature (°C), relative 
humidity (%), and a computed heat-index value. Screen 2 displays MQ-7 CO concentration 
(ppm), MQ-135 composite reading (ppm), and a three-level status indicator rendered as an 
inverted text block labelled SAFE, CAUTION, or DANGER. 
3.3  Circuit Design and Connections 
All components are powered from a regulated 5 V USB supply. The ESP32 
development board incorporates an on-board AMS1117-3.3 LDO voltage regulator that 
supplies the 3.3 V rail required by the SSD1306 OLED displays and the DHT22. The MQ-7 
and MQ-135 heater elements require 5 V and are connected direct

on-board AMS1117-3.3 LDO voltage regulator that 
supplies the 3.3 V rail required by the SSD1306 OLED displays and the DHT22. The MQ-7 
and MQ-135 heater elements require 5 V and are connected directly to the USB rail. Both 
sensor analogue outputs are attenuated through a resistive voltage divider to ensure the signal 
does not exceed the 3.3 V ADC reference of the ESP32. 
The buzzer is driven through a 2N2222 NPN transistor switch, with a 1 kΩ base resistor 
limiting current from the GPIO pin and a 1N4007 flyback diode protecting the transistor from 
inductive kickback during buzzer deactivation. A bicolour LED (green/red common-cathode) 
is connected to two independent GPIO pins, each through a 330 Ω current-limiting resistor, 
allowing independent assertion of the green (safe) and red (alarm) states without mutual 
interference.

follows a fixed 2-second sampling cycle that sequentially: (1) triggers a DHT22 acquisition 
and checks the one-wire CRC, (2) reads the MQ-7 and MQ-135 ADC channels as the average

4.4  Operational Stability 
A 72-hour continuous soak test was conducted at room temperature (25°C) with both 
Wi-Fi and HTTP serving active throughout. No thermal shutdown events, memory 
fragmentation faults, I²C bus lockups, or watchdog resets were recorded over the test period. 
OLED display brightness showed no observable degradation. Sensor readings drifted by less 
than 3% over the 72-hour period, consistent with the expected long-term drift specification for 
MQ-series sensors.

CHAPTER 5

5.1  Conclusion 
This project has successfully designed, implemented, and validated a Compact 
Embedded Monitoring System (CEMS) for industrial hazard detection. The prototype 
integrates simultaneous monitoring of carbon monoxide, broadband toxic gas index, 
temperature, and relative humidity within a single portable device centred on the ESP32 
microcontroller. Local real-time data visualisation is provided on dual SSD1306 OLED 
displays, supplemented by a Wi-Fi-hosted web dashboard that enables remote monitoring 
without dependence on cloud infrastructure. 
Experimental characterisation confirmed that MQ-7 CO measurements are accurate to 
within ±10% of a reference analyser across the 50–300 ppm range, DHT22 temperature and 
humidity readings agree with a calibrated reference instrument to within ±2%, and threshold 
alert latency averages 326 ms — comfortably within the 1-second guideline for industrial 
safety aler

and 
humidity readings agree with a calibrated reference instrument to within ±2%, and threshold 
alert latency averages 326 ms — comfortably within the 1-second guideline for industrial 
safety alerting. The device operates continuously at 218 mA from a standard 5 V USB supply 
and demonstrated stable performance across a 72-hour soak test. 
Compared with existing solutions reviewed in the literature, the CEMS prototype 
uniquely combines three-gas coverage, ambient environmental sensing, dual-OLED local 
display, infrastructure-independent Wi-Fi monitoring, and dual-modality alerting within a 
single low-cost design. The project thus demonstrates a viable hardware reference platform for 
the next generation of portable industrial safety monitors.
